title: Priests, Forbidden Practices, and a Prophet Like Moses
summary: Moses sets out the support of the Levitical priests, who own no land because the LORD is their inheritance. He forbids every form of divination, sorcery, child sacrifice, and consulting the dead, and promises instead that God will raise up a prophet like Moses. The chapter ends with a test for telling a true prophet from a false one.
story: Moses is still describing the offices that will lead Israel in the land. Chapter 16 dealt with judges, chapter 17 with the central court and the king, and now chapter 18 turns to the priests and the prophet. The chapter answers a practical question that every people in the ancient world faced: how do we know what the divine will is? Canaan's answer was divination and magic. Israel's answer is the word of God given through a prophet. The immediate reason is that Moses is about to die (his death comes in chapter 34), and the people need to know that God will keep speaking. The promise of a prophet like Moses echoed through the rest of the Bible, and by the time of Jesus it had become a hope for one particular prophet still to come.
historical:
The setting is again the plains of Moab before the crossing of the Jordan, with Moses addressing the whole assembly. The practices listed in verses 10-11 were real and widespread. Mesopotamian diviners read the livers of sacrificed sheep and recorded omens on clay tablets in large collections, and astrology, dream interpretation, and necromancy (consulting the dead) were practiced across the region. Israel's own later history shows how attractive these practices remained. King Saul, who had banned mediums, went to one at Endor on the night before his last battle (1 Samuel 28). The Judean kings Ahaz and Manasseh made their sons pass through the fire and practiced divination (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and the historians name these acts as the ways of the nations the LORD had driven out.

The hope for a prophet like Moses stayed alive long after the Old Testament closed. Deuteronomy's own final chapter says that no prophet had since arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face (34:10). Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a short collection of messianic proof texts from Qumran includes verses 18-19 of this chapter. In John's Gospel, people ask John the Baptist whether he is the Prophet and later say of Jesus that he must be the Prophet who was to come into the world (John 1:21; 6:14).
cultural:
The Levites had no tribal territory, only towns to live in scattered through the land, so they depended on the worship of Israel for their food. The shoulder, jowls, and stomach of sacrificed animals, the firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and the first shearing of wool were their portion. Verses 6-8 protect a country Levite who moves to the central sanctuary: he is to share equally with the priests already serving there, even if he has income from selling family property.

The forbidden practices in verses 10-11 are a deliberate catalogue. Some are ways of reading the future from signs (divination, interpreting omens), some are ways of controlling events by ritual power (sorcery, casting spells), and some are attempts to speak with the dead through a medium or spiritist. Child sacrifice heads the list because it was the most extreme form of the same instinct: to secure the future by paying the gods whatever price they demanded. Israel's God refuses to be managed. He speaks when he chooses and through whom he chooses, and his people are to listen.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined by a contrast. Verses 1-8 are regulations about priestly support, framed by the repeated statement that the LORD is their inheritance. Verses 9-22 are a sermon-like contrast between the nations, who listen to conjurers and diviners, and Israel, to whom God will raise up a prophet. The central promise is given twice, first in Moses' voice (verse 15) and then as God's own words recalled from Horeb (verse 18), moving from like me to like you. The passage looks back to the scene at Sinai in Deuteronomy 5, where the people begged Moses to stand between them and God's voice, and it closes with a question the reader might ask (verse 21) and its answer (verse 22), a teaching device Deuteronomy uses often.

outline.t: The LORD is the Levites' inheritance
Equal shares for a Levite who comes to the sanctuary
No divination, sorcery, or consulting the dead

doctrines.note: God makes himself known by speaking, not by being discovered through omens or manipulated through ritual. The prophet is defined as one in whose mouth God puts his words, and the people are accountable to listen.
Divination, magic, and child sacrifice are all ways of trying to control the unseen for our own ends. The chapter calls them detestable, and it gives Israel a better way: trusting a God who speaks.
The promise of a prophet like Moses became part of Israel's hope for a coming deliverer. The New Testament identifies Jesus as that prophet (Acts 3:22-23).

words.note: Navi, prophet. The core meaning is a spokesman, one who speaks on behalf of another. The chapter's definition is exact: God puts his words in the prophet's mouth, and the prophet tells the people everything God commands. A prophet is measured by faithfulness to the message, not by foretelling as such.

Nachalah, inheritance. Usually it means a family's allotted land, passed down through generations. The Levites receive none, and verse 2 says the LORD himself is their inheritance, a striking claim that the Psalms later take up in personal prayer.

Tamim, whole, complete, or blameless. The same word describes a sacrificial animal without defect. In verse 13 it describes a people who are undivided in their loyalty, trusting the LORD entirely rather than hedging their bets with the spirits of the land.

Qasam, to practice divination. The word covers attempts to discover hidden knowledge through signs, lots, or omens. It stands first among the practices Israel is to reject, and later prophets use it for the false seers who told Israel what it wanted to hear.

christ: This is one of the clearest Old Testament promises that the New Testament applies to Jesus. Peter, preaching in the temple after Pentecost, quotes the promise and identifies Jesus as the prophet like Moses whom the people must hear (Acts 3:22-23), and Stephen cites it in his defense (Acts 7:37). At the transfiguration, when Moses himself appears with Jesus, the voice from the cloud commands the disciples to listen to him (Matthew 17:5), which echoes verse 15. Scholars debate whether the passage originally promised a single future figure or a line of prophets raised up in each generation; many see both, with the line of prophets pointing forward to one who would complete it. Hebrews draws the contrast: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ as a son over it (Hebrews 3:5-6). The people at Horeb asked for a mediator because they could not bear God's voice directly. In Jesus, Christians confess, God has given the mediator who speaks God's words because he is himself the Word.

hard.q: Is fulfillment really the test of a true prophet, when some biblical prophecies did not come to pass as spoken?
hard.a:
Verse 22 gives a negative test: if a prophet's word fails, the LORD has not spoken it. But the Bible itself records prophecies that were not carried out, most famously Jonah's announcement that Nineveh would be overturned, which God relented from when the city repented. Jeremiah 18 explains the principle: many announcements of judgment or blessing carry an unstated condition, and God may relent if a nation turns. Interpreters therefore read verse 22 as applying to a prophet's plain claims rather than to warnings meant to provoke repentance.

The test also isn't the only one. Deuteronomy 13 warns that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads Israel after other gods. Fulfillment is necessary but not sufficient; faithfulness to the LORD and his covenant is the deeper test. Read together, the two chapters give Israel a way to reject impostors without treating every prediction as a simple forecast.

questions: Divination and magic were ways of trying to control an uncertain future. What do people today use to feel in control of what lies ahead?
The Levites had no land and lived on what God's people gave. What would it mean for you to say that the LORD is your inheritance?
Deuteronomy gives Israel tests for telling a true word from a false one. How do you weigh the voices that claim to speak for God?
